items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "activation energy"?
options: The temporary structure formed when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme.
The hypothesis that the substrate fits exactly into a rigid active site with a complementary shape.
The energy that must be supplied to make a reaction start.
The hypothesis that the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, so that it fits more closely around the substrate.
items.answer: The energy that must be supplied to make a reaction start.
items.markingKey: Activation energy: the energy that must be supplied to make a reaction start.

items.stem: Compare the lock-and-key and induced-fit hypotheses of enzyme action.
items.answer: Both: substrate binds to a specific active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex. Lock-and-key: active site rigid, exactly complementary. Induced fit: active site changes shape slightly as substrate binds, moulding round it and putting strain on bonds.
items.markingKey: similarity [1]; lock-and-key rigid [1]; induced fit shape change [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how the formation of an enzyme–substrate complex lowers the activation energy.
items.answer: Binding holds substrates close together in the correct orientation, or the change in shape strains bonds in the substrate, so they break more easily.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Binding holds substrates close together in the correct orientation; or the change in shape strains bonds in the substrate; so they break more easily (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: The activation energy for the hydrolysis of sucrose is 200 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 49 kJ mol⁻¹ with an enzyme. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in activation energy. (b) Sketch or describe an energy-level diagram for the reaction with and without the enzyme.
items.answer: (a) 75.5% (b) Same starting and end energy levels; the enzyme curve has a lower peak; activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak.
items.markingKey: (a) (200 − 49) ÷ 200 × 100 = 75.5% [2] (b) lower peak with enzyme [1]; same energy of reactants / products [1] [4]

items.stem: The activation energy for the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide is 75 kJ mol⁻¹ without a catalyst and 40 kJ mol⁻¹ with an enzyme. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in activation energy. (b) Sketch or describe an energy-level diagram for the reaction with and without the enzyme. (c) Explain how the enzyme lowers the activation energy.
items.answer: (a) 46.7% (b) Same starting and end energy levels; the enzyme curve has a lower peak; activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak. (c) The substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex; induced fit strains bonds or holds reactants together so bonds break / form more easily.
items.markingKey: (a) (75 − 40) ÷ 75 × 100 = 46.7% [2] (b) lower peak with enzyme [1]; same energy of reactants / products [1] (c) E–S complex [1]; strain / orientation [1] [6]

items.stem: Sucrase catalyses the breakdown of sucrose into glucose and fructose. Researchers in Madrid used X-ray crystallography and found that the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds. (a) Explain why the enzyme cannot catalyse the breakdown of other substrates. (b) Explain why a mutation changing one amino acid far from the active site might still stop the enzyme working.
items.answer: (a) The active site has a specific shape complementary only to its substrate (determined by tertiary structure); other substrates cannot bind / form an E–S complex. (b) It can change bonding between R groups, so the tertiary structure and active site shape change.
items.markingKey: (a) The active site has a specific shape complementary only to its substrate (determined by tertiary structure) [1]; other substrates cannot bind / form an E–S complex [1] [2] (b) It can change bonding between R groups [1]; so the tertiary structure and active site shape change [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an enzyme can be used again and again.
items.answer: It is not changed by the reaction; after products leave the active site, it is free to bind another substrate.
items.markingKey: It is not changed by the reaction [1]; after products leave the active site, it is free to bind another substrate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the tertiary structure of an enzyme is essential to its function.
items.answer: The tertiary structure (held by bonds between R groups) determines the 3-D shape of the active site, which must be complementary to the substrate.
items.markingKey: The tertiary structure (held by bonds between R groups) determines the 3-D shape of the active site [1]; which must be complementary to the substrate [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Jakarta states: "Enzymes provide energy for reactions." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Enzymes lower the activation energy; they do not supply energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Enzymes lower the activation energy; they do not supply energy. [2]

items.stem: Omar measured the reducing sugar produced by an enzyme reaction. Time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10. Total reducing sugar / mg: 0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.1, 3.9, 5.4, 6.5, 7.5. (a) Calculate the mean rate in the first minute. (b) Calculate the mean rate between 2 and 8 minutes. (c) Explain why the rate decreases with time.
items.answer: (a) 1.1 mg min⁻¹ (b) 0.72 mg min⁻¹ (c) Substrate is used up, so there are fewer enzyme–substrate collisions per unit time and fewer E–S complexes form.
items.markingKey: (a) 1.1 [1] (b) (6.5 − 2.2) ÷ 6 = 0.72 [2] (c) substrate concentration falls [1]; fewer collisions / E–S complexes [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain how enzymes catalyse reactions, with reference to the lock-and-key and induced-fit hypotheses and to activation energy.
items.answer: Globular proteins with active site; tertiary structure gives specific shape; substrate collides and binds forming E–S complex; lock-and-key rigid fit vs induced fit shape change; strain / orientation lowers activation energy; products released; enzyme unchanged.
items.markingKey: active site / specificity [2]; E–S complex [1]; two hypotheses contrasted [2]; activation energy [1] [6]

items.stem: Lysozyme catalyses the breakdown of peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls into smaller sugar fragments. Researchers in Accra used X-ray crystallography and found that the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds. (a) Explain why the enzyme cannot catalyse the breakdown of other substrates. (b) Explain why a mutation changing one amino acid far from the active site might still stop the enzyme working. (c) Draw or describe an energy diagram showing the effect of the enzyme.
items.answer: (a) The active site has a specific shape complementary only to its substrate (determined by tertiary structure); other substrates cannot bind / form an E–S complex. (b) It can change bonding between R groups, so the tertiary structure and active site shape change. (c) Reaction profile with lower activation energy peak with enzyme; same overall energy change.
items.markingKey: (a) The active site has a specific shape complementary only to its substrate (determined by tertiary structure) [1]; other substrates cannot bind / form an E–S complex [1] [2] (b) It can change bonding between R groups [1]; so the tertiary structure and active site shape change [1] [2] (c) Reaction profile with lower activation energy peak with enzyme [1]; same overall energy change [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "the factor in shortest supply, which limits the rate of a reaction"?
options: Temperature coefficient (Q10)
Optimum pH
Buffer solution
Limiting factor
items.answer: Limiting factor
items.markingKey: Limiting factor: the factor in shortest supply, which limits the rate of a reaction.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction falls rapidly above the optimum temperature.
items.answer: Increased vibration breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the tertiary structure; the active site changes shape so substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is denatured and fewer E–S complexes form.
items.markingKey: bonds break [1]; active site shape changes [1]; fewer E–S complexes / denatured [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain the effect of increasing enzyme concentration on the rate of reaction when substrate is in excess.
items.answer: More active sites are available, so more E–S complexes form per unit time; rate increases in proportion to enzyme concentration.
items.markingKey: More active sites are available, so more E–S complexes form per unit time [1]; rate increases in proportion to enzyme concentration [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 0.7, 4.8, 15.5, 23.1, 15.4, 4.9; trial 2: 0.7, 4.9, 16, 23.2, 15.8, 4.8; trial 3: 0.7, 4.9, 15.1, 22.8, 15.4, 5. Calculate the temperature coefficient Q10 between the two lowest temperatures tested.

Freya added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 0.7, 4.9, 15, 13.3, 15.1, 4.8; trial 2: 0.7, 4.8, 14.8, 23.2, 15.2, 4.9; trial 3: 0.7, 4.7, 15.7, 22.9, 15.1, 4.7. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute. (b) Use a thermostatically controlled water bath.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use a thermostatically controlled water bath; pre-incubate the enzyme and substrate separately at the test temperature; use a gas syringe rather than counting bubbles; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Mohammed added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 2.1, 9.7, 21.9, 21.9, 10, 2.2; trial 2: 3.2, 10, 21.1, 22, 9.8, 2.1; trial 3: 2.2, 9.9, 21.8, 22.1, 9.9, 2.1. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute at 45 °C, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: (a) Volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide; volume and concentration of catalase extract. (b) 22 cm³
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide; volume and concentration of catalase extract; pH (use a buffer); time allowed to equilibrate in the water bath; collection time [2] (b) (21.9 + 22 + 22.1) ÷ 3 [1] = 22 cm³ [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 0.8, 5, 16, 34.8, 16.6, 5.2; trial 2: 0.7, 5, 16.6, 23.2, 15.5, 5.1; trial 3: 0.7, 5.1, 16, 24, 16.3, 5.2. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) The volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute increases as the temperature rises to 40 °C, which gives the highest value, then decreases. (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 5, 15.6, 22.1, 21.8, 5; trial 2: 4.7, 15.7, 21.8, 15.2, 5; trial 3: 5, 15, 23.1, 15.1, 5. (a) Explain the results. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: (a) As temperature rises to the optimum, molecules have more kinetic energy so more E–S complexes form per second; above the optimum, hydrogen bonds in the enzyme break, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured. (b) Use boiled (denatured) catalase extract with hydrogen peroxide at each temperature; little oxygen should be produced, showing that oxygen production is due to the active enzyme.
items.markingKey: (a) kinetic energy / collisions [1]; optimum [1]; denaturation and active site shape [1] [3] (b) 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "optimum pH"?
options: The factor by which the rate of a reaction increases for a 10 °C rise in temperature.
The pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
The factor in shortest supply, which limits the rate of a reaction.
A solution that resists changes in pH, used to keep pH constant in enzyme investigations.
items.answer: The pH at which an enzyme works fastest.
items.markingKey: Optimum pH: the pH at which an enzyme works fastest.

items.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction increase from 10 °C to 30 °C?
options: Activation energy increases
More enzyme molecules are made
Molecules have more kinetic energy so collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent
The active site gets larger
items.answer: Molecules have more kinetic energy so collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent
items.markingKey: More kinetic energy → more successful collisions and E–S complexes.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of reaction levels off as substrate concentration increases.
items.answer: At high substrate concentration all active sites are occupied at any moment (saturated); enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor; the rate reaches Vmax.
items.markingKey: active sites saturated [1]; enzyme limiting [1]; Vmax [1] [3]

items.stem: Daniel mixed amylase with starch solution in buffers of different pH at 35 °C. Every 10 s a drop of the mixture was tested with iodine solution on a spotting tile, and the time taken until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. pH: 5, 6, 7, 8. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 131, 58, 41, 83; trial 2: 137, 57, 41, 79; trial 3: 134, 59, 40, 82. Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: Use boiled amylase (or water instead of amylase) with starch at each pH; the iodine should stay blue-black, showing starch breakdown is caused by the enzyme.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2]

items.stem: Felix added trypsin solutions of different concentrations to milk-powder suspension at 30 °C and recorded the time for the suspension to become clear as casein was hydrolysed. Results table. Trypsin concentration / %: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Time for milk to clear / s, trial 1: 275, 134, 88, 69; trial 2: 259, 138, 89, 68; trial 3: 263, 135, 131, 67. Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: Use boiled trypsin solution with the milk suspension; it should not clear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2]

items.stem: Hana added 2 cm³ of catalase extract (from celery) to 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution at pH 7, and collected the oxygen in a gas syringe for 1 minute at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65. Volume of oxygen collected in 1 minute / cm³, trial 1: 2, 9.5, 20.2, 18.9, 9.3, 1.9; trial 2: 2, 9.2, 20.3, 20, 9.4, 2; trial 3: 2, 9.5, 19.8, 19, 9.4, 1.9. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) Calculate the temperature coefficient Q10 between the two lowest temperatures tested.
items.answer: (a) Use a thermostatically controlled water bath. (b) 4.7
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: use a thermostatically controlled water bath; pre-incubate the enzyme and substrate separately at the test temperature; use a gas syringe rather than counting bubbles; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) Q10 = rate at (T + 10) ÷ rate at T = 9.4 ÷ 2 = 4.7 [2]

items.stem: Omar mixed amylase with starch solution in buffers of different pH at 35 °C. Every 10 s a drop of the mixture was tested with iodine solution on a spotting tile, and the time taken until the iodine no longer turned blue-black was recorded. Results table. pH: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Time for starch to disappear / s, trial 1: 230, 120, 53, 36, 69, 156; trial 2: 224, 115, 51, 23, 72, 162; trial 3: 230, 120, 51, 37, 74, 162. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Trial 2 at pH 7 (23 s); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Test more frequently (e.g. every 5 s) to reduce the uncertainty in the end point. (c) A line graph: pH on the x-axis and mean time for starch to disappear on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 2 at pH 7 identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: test more frequently (e.g. every 5 s) to reduce the uncertainty in the end point; use a colorimeter to judge the end point objectively; use a narrower range of pH near the optimum; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the pH (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (c) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; pH on x-axis and time for starch to disappear on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel added trypsin solutions of different concentrations to milk-powder suspension at 30 °C and recorded the time for the suspension to become clear as casein was hydrolysed. Results table. Trypsin concentration / %: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Time for milk to clear / s, trial 1: 233, 116, 107, 54; trial 2: 228, 113, 76, 56; trial 3: 233, 114, 72, 56. (a) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed. (c) Calculate the rate of reaction (1 ÷ time) for the highest trypsin concentration, in s⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) Use a colorimeter to measure the end point. (b) Use boiled trypsin solution with the milk suspension; it should not clear. (c) 0.0181 s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) Any one from: use a colorimeter to measure the end point; place a printed cross behind the tube and record when it becomes visible; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the trypsin concentration (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (b) 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: shows that the change is caused by the independent variable [2] (c) 1 ÷ 55.3 = 0.0181 s⁻¹ [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the control of a metabolic pathway in which the final product inhibits an enzyme earlier in the pathway"?
options: End-product inhibition
Non-competitive inhibitor
Reversible inhibitor
Competitive inhibitor
items.answer: End-product inhibition
items.markingKey: End-product inhibition: the control of a metabolic pathway in which the final product inhibits an enzyme earlier in the pathway.

items.stem: Explain why increasing the substrate concentration overcomes competitive inhibition but not non-competitive inhibition.
items.answer: Competitive inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site; more substrate means more likely to bind than the inhibitor. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the active site, so substrate cannot bind whatever its concentration.
items.markingKey: competition for active site [1]; more substrate wins [1]; non-competitive changes active site shape [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how end-product inhibition controls a metabolic pathway.
items.answer: The end product binds (non-competitively, at an allosteric site) to an enzyme early in the pathway, reducing its activity; when the product is used up, the inhibition is removed. This prevents waste of resources.
items.markingKey: The end product binds (non-competitively, at an allosteric site) to an enzyme early in the pathway, reducing its activity [1]; when the product is used up, the inhibition is removed [1]; This prevents waste of resources [1] [3]

items.stem: Hana measured the initial rate of an enzyme reaction (μmol min⁻¹) at different substrate concentrations (mmol dm⁻³), with and without substance X. Substrate concentration: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Rate without X: 16, 26.7, 40, 53.3, 64, 71.1. Rate with X: 5.3, 8.9, 13.3, 17.8, 21.3, 23.7. Describe how the data would appear on a graph of rate against substrate concentration.
items.answer: Both curves rise then level off; with X the curve levels off at a lower maximum (Vmax reduced).
items.markingKey: Both curves rise then level off [1]; with X the curve levels off at a lower maximum (Vmax reduced) [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace measured the initial rate of an enzyme reaction (μmol min⁻¹) at different substrate concentrations (mmol dm⁻³), with and without substance X. Substrate concentration: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Rate without X: 16, 26.7, 40, 53.3, 64, 71.1. Rate with X: 7.3, 13.3, 22.9, 35.6, 49.2, 61. (a) Explain how X reduces the rate of reaction. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant.
items.answer: (a) X has a similar shape to the substrate and binds to the active site, so fewer E–S complexes form. (b) Temperature; pH; enzyme concentration; concentration of X.
items.markingKey: (a) X has a similar shape to the substrate and binds to the active site [1]; so fewer E–S complexes form [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Temperature; pH; enzyme concentration; concentration of X (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: In a hospital in Jakarta, captopril is used for reducing high blood pressure. It inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), and its effect is reduced when the concentration of the normal substrate is high. (a) Explain why a drug that acts as a non-competitive inhibitor would not be reversed by adding substrate. (b) Describe the effect of the drug on the Vmax and on the substrate concentration needed to reach half Vmax.
items.answer: (a) It binds elsewhere and changes active site shape; substrate cannot bind regardless of concentration. (b) Vmax unchanged; higher substrate concentration needed to reach Vmax/2 (apparent Km increases).
items.markingKey: (a) It binds elsewhere and changes active site shape [1]; substrate cannot bind regardless of concentration [1] [2] (b) Vmax unchanged [1]; higher substrate concentration needed to reach Vmax/2 (apparent Km increases) [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the effect of increasing substrate concentration on the inhibition caused by a competitive inhibitor?
options: The inhibition increases
There is no effect
The enzyme is denatured
The inhibition is reduced
items.answer: The inhibition is reduced
items.markingKey: Substrate out-competes inhibitor for active sites; Vmax can still be reached.

items.stem: Explain why heavy-metal ions such as mercury are non-competitive inhibitors.
items.answer: They bind to –SH groups of R groups away from the active site, disrupting bonds (e.g. disulfide bonds) and changing the tertiary structure and active site shape.
items.markingKey: They bind to –SH groups of R groups away from the active site [1]; disrupting bonds (e.g. disulfide bonds) and changing the tertiary structure and active site shape [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana says: "Competitive inhibitors permanently denature the enzyme." Explain whether Ana is correct.
items.answer: Competitive inhibitors usually bind reversibly and do not change the enzyme's shape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Competitive inhibitors usually bind reversibly and do not change the enzyme's shape. [2]

items.stem: Ethan measured the initial rate of an enzyme reaction (μmol min⁻¹) at different substrate concentrations (mmol dm⁻³), with and without substance X. Substrate concentration: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Rate without X: 33.3, 50, 66.7, 80, 88.9, 94.1. Rate with X: 14.3, 25, 40, 57.1, 72.7, 84.2. Calculate the percentage inhibition at the lowest and highest substrate concentrations.

Elena measured the initial rate of an enzyme reaction (μmol min⁻¹) at different substrate concentrations (mmol dm⁻³), with and without substance X. Substrate concentration: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Rate without X: 12.5, 20, 28.6, 36.4, 42.1, 45.7. Rate with X: 4.2, 6.7, 9.5, 12.1, 14, 15.2. (a) Explain how X reduces the rate of reaction. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant.
items.answer: (a) X binds at a site other than the active site, changing the tertiary structure and shape of the active site so substrate cannot bind. (b) Temperature; pH; enzyme concentration; concentration of X.
items.markingKey: (a) X binds at a site other than the active site [1]; changing the tertiary structure and shape of the active site so substrate cannot bind [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Temperature; pH; enzyme concentration; concentration of X (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "Michaelis–Menten constant (Km)"?
options: A polysaccharide from seaweed that forms beads in calcium chloride solution, used to immobilise enzymes.
An enzyme held in an inert matrix such as alginate beads, so that it can be reused and kept separate from the product.
The substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its maximum rate (½Vmax).
How readily an enzyme binds to its substrate; a low Km indicates a high affinity.
items.answer: The substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its maximum rate (½Vmax).
items.markingKey: Michaelis–Menten constant (Km): the substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its maximum rate (½Vmax).

items.stem: Explain why an immobilised enzyme may give a lower rate than the same enzyme free in solution.
items.answer: Substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the active sites, and some active sites are inaccessible, so fewer collisions occur per unit time.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the active sites; and some active sites are inaccessible; so fewer collisions occur per unit time (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Explain why immobilised enzymes are often more stable at high temperatures.
items.answer: The matrix holds the enzyme molecules and restricts changes in shape, so the tertiary structure is less easily disrupted.
items.markingKey: The matrix holds the enzyme molecules and restricts changes in shape [1]; so the tertiary structure is less easily disrupted [1] [2]

items.stem: The initial rate of reaction of lactase was measured at different substrate concentrations. Substrate / mmol dm⁻³: 1, 2, 4, 8, 20, 40, 80. Rate / μmol min⁻¹: 16, 26.7, 40, 53.3, 66.7, 72.7, 76.2. Vmax was found to be 80 μmol min⁻¹. (a) State the rate that corresponds to ½Vmax. (b) Use the data to find Km.
items.answer: (a) 40 μmol min⁻¹ (b) 4 mmol dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) 80 ÷ 2 = 40 [1] (b) substrate concentration at rate 40 = 4 mmol dm⁻³ [1] [2]

items.stem: The initial rate of reaction of invertase was measured at different substrate concentrations. Substrate / mmol dm⁻³: 1, 2, 4, 8, 20, 40, 80. Rate / μmol min⁻¹: 4.8, 8, 12, 16, 20, 21.8, 22.9. Vmax was found to be 24 μmol min⁻¹. (a) State the rate that corresponds to ½Vmax. (b) Use the data to find Km. (c) A second enzyme catalysing the same reaction has Km = 20 mmol dm⁻³. Compare the affinities of the two enzymes for the substrate.
items.answer: (a) 12 μmol min⁻¹ (b) 4 mmol dm⁻³ (c) Invertase has the lower Km and so the higher affinity: it reaches half its maximum rate at a lower substrate concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) 24 ÷ 2 = 12 [1] (b) substrate concentration at rate 12 = 4 mmol dm⁻³ [1] (c) lower Km identified [1]; higher affinity explained [1] [4]

items.stem: Arjun packed lactase immobilised in alginate beads into a column and passed milk through at different flow rates, testing the glucose concentration of the product with test strips. Results table. Flow rate of milk / cm³ min⁻¹: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8. Glucose concentration in product / mmol dm⁻³, trial 1: 22.6, 17.5, 12.7, 9.9, 4.8; trial 2: 21.7, 17.5, 12.5, 10, 7.7; trial 3: 22.1, 18.4, 12.4, 9.6, 7.8. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Describe a suitable control for this investigation and explain why it is needed.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 8 cm³ min⁻¹ (4.8 mmol dm⁻³); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Pass milk through a column of alginate beads made without lactase; no glucose should be detected, showing the enzyme is responsible.

items.stem: Explain why enzymes from organisms living in hot springs have higher optimum temperatures.

Non-competitive
